# Draft:Renaissance Philanthropy

----
Renaissance Philanthropy is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization founded in 2024 that specializes in philanthropic advisory services, designing and managing time-bound, thesis-driven funds to leverage science, technology, and innovation for addressing societal challenges and advising philanthropists on high-impact giving. By increasing ambition in science, technology, and innovation, and advising donors on supporting breakthrough giving, it aims to fuel a “21st century renaissance” and create a “brighter future for all through science, technology, and innovation.”

In its inaugural year (2024-2025), the organization catalyzed over $214 million in funding, including $162 million matched to high-impact organizations and $52 million committed to more than 10 new programs and funds, while tripling its team size and launching global initiatives.
History
Renaissance Philanthropy was launched on May 6, 2024, by Tom Kalil and Kumar Garg, both former officials in the Obama administration’s White House Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP). Kalil served as deputy director for policy at OSTP and later as chief innovation officer at Schmidt Futures, while Garg was managing director at Schmidt Futures and assistant director at OSTP. The organization emerged from their experiences in government and philanthropy, aiming to create new models for supporting ambitious science and technology projects that fall outside traditional funding mechanisms. Initial funding was provided by Eric and Wendy Schmidt.
By the end of 2025, the organization released its first annual report, highlighting $162 million matched to high-impact organizations and $52 million committed to over 10 programs and funds it launched. The report also noted the tripling of its core team and the launch of initiatives in multiple domains.
Mission and activities
The core mission of Renaissance Philanthropy is to design and implement ambitious philanthropic efforts that advance entire fields through science, technology, and innovation, creating a “virtuous loop” of increasing ambition and impact between philanthropists and innovators. It focuses on building time-bound, thesis-driven funds that allow donors to support high-impact ideas without establishing large internal teams, targeting projects too large for academia or not profitable enough for venture capital.
Core thesis areas include AI in mathematics and education, climate, health and biomedical discovery, scientific infrastructure, talent mobility and immigration, and public benefit innovation.
Key activities include:
* Providing “playbooks” as open-source toolkits for high-impact, counterfactual giving, covering topics like commitments, policy entrepreneurship, and scientific field creation. Ten playbooks were published by the end of 2025.
* Catalyzing funds for specific initiatives, such as the AI for Math Fund, which announced $18 million in grants with XTX Markets to accelerate breakthroughs in mathematics through open-source tools, datasets, and infrastructure.
* Launching the AI and Education Fund, backed by the Walton Family Foundation and Schultz Family Foundation, focusing on AI-driven student success, including a tools competition, a foundry for idea incubation, and AI moonshots like the Learning Engineering Virtual Institute (LEVI) math program.
* Developing the Talent Mobility Fund to expand access to STEM immigration pathways.
* Partnering with the Japan Cabinet Office and Japan Science and Technology Agency to launch the ASCENT Program for international collaboration in science and technology.
* Running the Big if True Science (BiTS) Accelerator to train scientists in designing large-scale research programs, with cohorts in the UK, EU, Africa, the Americas, and Japan, supported by partners like Coefficient Giving.
* Launching the UK Horizons Programme in partnership with the Advanced Research and Invention Agency (ARIA), including components like the Alliance of Talent Leaders Across Science (ATLAS), Higgs Community, and Climate Emergencies Forum.
* Launching the Advanced Research for Climate Emergencies (ARC) program, which funds cutting-edge research and strategic partnerships to predict, prevent, and prepare for catastrophic climate risks, including efforts to prevent sea level rise, mitigate climate overshoot, restore ocean ecosystems, and build resilience through areas like ice sheet stabilization, ocean nutrient enhancement, and emergency response innovations.
The organization also shares insights through publications, Q&As, discussions, and policy recommendations on topics like AI in biomedical discovery, climate solutions, formal mathematics, court innovation, education, industrial policy, metascience, and autonomous science instruments.
Leadership and team
Tom Kalil serves as CEO, with extensive experience from the White House OSTP, Schmidt Futures, and initiatives like the National Nanotechnology Initiative and BRAIN Initiative. Kumar Garg serves as President, with prior roles at OSTP and Schmidt Futures, focusing on partnerships and policy.
The team comprises former White House and DARPA leaders, domain experts, engineers, entrepreneurs, and program designers, having collectively programmed $1B+ in DARPA programs and catalyzed $61B through multi-sector consortia.
Partnerships and funding
Renaissance Philanthropy collaborates with entities such as the Advanced Research and Invention Agency (ARIA), Eric and Wendy Schmidt, Walton Family Foundation, Schultz Family Foundation, Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation, XTX Markets, Coefficient Giving, Japan Science and Technology Agency (JST), the Japan Cabinet Office, and Deep Science Ventures. The organization targets emerging high-net-worth donors to increase philanthropic giving in science and tech.
